transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: available
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Rao (Redwood SE), Lina Morales (Redwood SE), Marta Diaz (Cerulean Head of ML), Devon Park (Cerulean SRE), Ibrahim Khan (Platform), Priya Singh (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
- Deep dive on autoscale: Cerulean wants bounded p95 latency during morning peak while supporting 8x burst factor for overnight Black Friday-style events.
- Focus on prewarmed pools, concurrency throttles, queueing windows, and guaranteed reserved GPU sizing.
- Discussed KV cache warmup, batching/latency tradeoffs, and quantization as cost lever.
- Next: share burst sim workbook; customer to provide traces; Redwood to propose prewarm policy for pilot.

Transcript:
[00:00] Avery (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll, then Samir will take us into the sim and the prewarm idea.
[00:12] Marta (Cerulean): Hi, Marta here. We run inference for routing/ETA suggestions, so tight p95 matters. We see big morning and evening spikes, sometimes sudden truck-fleet rebalancing alerts.
[00:25] Devon: Devon here — SRE, I support the infra side and we need predictable tail latency and isolation from other workloads.
[00:34] Avery: Great. Samir?
[00:36] Samir (Redwood SE): Yep. I'll share my screen with a high-level model. Quick caveat: the workbook is a simulation — not a guarantee but helps size reserved pools and prewarmed instances.
[01:05] Samir: So Cerulean's ask was: keep p95 under 220ms for shortest flows, allow burst up to 6-8x traffic, and not blow monthly GPU budget. Right? (murmur)
[01:18] Marta: That's right. Ideally we keep cost delta under 30% vs our current host pool.
[01:25] Ibrahim: And we have a VPC, KMS, and we want no egress of payloads, so private deployment constraints apply.
[01:33] Samir: Good — that maps to Redwood Private. Two knobs we tune: (1) reserved prewarmed pool size, and (2) concurrency throttles + queue window.
[01:46] Lina (Redwood): I'll add KV cache warmup as a third important piece — if your prefix hits are high, warm caches drastically reduce per-request token latency.
[01:57] Devon: Quick question — how do you do prewarm? Is that pinned GPU instances sitting idle? We can't afford 100% idle time.
[02:07] Samir: Right. Prewarm is configurable: you can set prewarmed replicas (hot GPUs with process warmed, KV cache state optionally persisted), plus a burst-queue capacity. The engines support ephemeral warmups too — short-lived additional replicas that spin up quickly but are less performant until KV cache warms.
[02:25] Marta: What's the warmup time for KV cache? Like how long until p95 improves?
[02:30] Samir: Depends on KV hit ratio and sequence lengths. If you're doing lots of short prompts with common prefixes, 5-20 seconds of traffic can warm a replica. For long-tail prefixes it might be minutes. We measure warmup by effective token reuse and early-offset KPIs.
[02:52] Ibrahim: So if a new model version rolls, do we lose all KV cache and have to re-warm?
[02:57] Lina: If model changes are weight-compatible (same architecture and tokenizer), Redwood supports cache prepopulation from a checkpoint or using synthetic warmup traffic — we can replay a small corpus to pre-populate hot keys. But full compatibility depends.
[03:16] Devon: Ok, show us the queueing model you use.
[03:19] Samir: Sure. On the slide: we model arrival as non-homogeneous Poisson with diurnal factors. Service time is a mixture distribution: short (<50 tokens) and long (>500 tokens) tails. We set a concurrency throttle per-VM and a system-level queue window.
[03:34] Samir: The throttle ensures that an individual VM doesn't take more than X concurrent requests to avoid KV thrash. If concurrent inflight requests exceeds reserved capacity, we either route to prewarmed pool, or put requests into a bounded priority queue with a user-configured max queue time (SLA window).
[03:50] Marta: If the queue exceeds the window, what's the fallback? Reject, degrade to smaller model, or spill to hosted?
[03:57] Samir: All are possible. Typical enterprise policy: try model fallback to a smaller/quantized variant, then if still overloaded, fail gracefully with a 503 and client-side retry. Redwood supports automatic fallback chains.
[04:10] Priya: For our use, fail-fast is better than delaying a routing decision. So we prefer a shorter queue window and small-model fallback.
[04:18] Samir: That's consistent. In the workbook I'll include tradeoff curves for p95 vs cost across queue window sizes and fallback policies.
[04:27] [05:00] (screen share changes)
[05:12] Samir: Here is a sample sim run: baseline traffic, 2 reserved GPUs (A100-ish equiv), prewarm 1 replica, burst factor 6, queue window 250ms, concurrency per VM set to 8. Outcome: p50=90ms, p95=310ms (over target).
[05:34] Marta: 310 is higher than our 220 target. What did you change to hit 220?
[05:38] Samir: Increase reserved pool to 4 GPUs and prewarm 2 replicas or decrease per-VM concurrency to 4 and add burst queue capacity. Either increases cost.
[05:48] Lina: Also quantization to int8 lowers token latency on some kernels but can increase model compute variance; it reduces cost per token and can let you run more replicas for same $$, which indirectly improves tail. We'll show quantized perf numbers later.
[06:03] Devon: There's also kernel variance on different GPU types. Our infra prefers lower cost VMs, but we'd prefer determinism. Any recommendations?
[06:12] Samir: For deterministic tail, prefer fewer large GPUs with higher single-rep throughput vs many small ones. The runtime optimizes kernel selection on startup; differences show up mainly on long sequences and attention memory pressure.
[06:25] Ibrahim: About prewarming persistence — you mentioned persisting KV cache state. Is that stored on disk attached to the instance? How is it restored on redeploy?
[06:33] Lina: We snapshot KV cache to a secure store in the same VPC (or S3-like object storage behind VPC endpoint). On redeploy, snapshot restores to new replica; restore is parallelized to reduce restore time. Note: snapshots add storage and restore costs.
[06:48] Marta: Can we limit which requests use prewarmed pool? For example high-value customers only.
[06:53] Samir: Yes — routing policies support token-based or route-level tagging; you can pin certain clients to reserved lanes and keep best-effort traffic on shared pools.
[07:04] Priya: Let's talk about throttles — how do you calculate concurrency per VM safely? Our workloads are mixed: 60% short, 40% long.
[07:12] Samir: We compute an effective service time E[S] from your trace; then concurrency_cap = floor(GPU_throughput / (E[S] * safety_factor)). In practice we recommend starting with conservative cap (4-6) and ramp after observing tail. The sim uses M/G/c approximations but we also run microbenchmarks.
[07:32] Marta: M/G/c — ok, so are you modeling queue as finite or infinite? We care about tail behavior when sudden surge happens.
[07:38] Samir: Bounded queue. We use finite buffer models with priority classes; beyond buffer we apply overflow policy. The buffer sizing ties directly to SLA window.
[07:48] Devon: Could you talk about burst policy: do you rely on cloud autoscale or Redwood-managed burst pools? Our clusters have cold-start penalties.
[07:56] Samir: Redwood Dedicated supports a hybrid: reserved prewarmed pool + ephemeral burst pool. Ephemeral nodes spin up faster because of optimized instance images and fewer init steps, but still need KV warmups. So we bake in a probabilistic warmup penalty. For strict SLO, rely mainly on prewarmed replicas and lower queue windows with model fallback.
[08:13] Ibrahim: For on-prem, spin-up times are longer — we might need more prewarm capacity.
[08:18] Lina: Exactly — on-prem typically needs a higher baseline of prewarmed units because hardware allocation and provisioning times are slower. The sim will show sensitivity to spin-up time parameter.
[08:28] [09:00] (customer muted while reading slide)
[09:10] Samir: Now quantization: int8 vs fp16. Int8 reduces memory and often improves throughput, but some kernels have slower int8 attention; plus quality can drop on few prompts. Best practice: use int8 for lower-cost tiers and keep fp16 for high-value flows — auto-fallback possible.
[09:33] Marta: Do you have quality regression detection built-in? We have strict QA before changing model numeric format.
[09:38] Lina: Redwood Optimize integrates quality monitors tied to prompt sets and evals; we'll trigger regression alarms if metric drift exceeds threshold. We recommend a small canary group for quantized models.
[09:50] Priya: On the Private side, KMS integration — will Redwood need key access? We can't give private keys off-VPC.
[09:57] Samir: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM; keys stay in your account and the control plane performs operations via delegated APIs. We can provide an architecture doc.
[10:10] Marta: Good. Regarding cost, how do you show cost curves in sim? We need explicit $/p95 at different reserved sizes.
[10:17] Samir: The workbook has cost per GPU-hour assumptions, plus cost of storage for KV snapshots, and estimated ops cost for prewarm snapshots. We'll parameterize your cloud prices.
[10:26] Devon: A real-world ask: during last year's flash sale our traffic spiked 9x and we saw p95 blow up to >2s for some routes. How would Redwood handle 9x?
[10:36] Samir: Two strategies: (A) prewarmed buffer sized to expected worst-case; (B) dynamic spill to hosted fallback (if allowed), with aggressive model fallback chain. For 9x you'd likely need a combination: larger prewarm plus smaller fallback models or reject flows. Workbook shows both scenarios.
[10:54] Marta: What about multi-region routing? Can we route traffic to different regions if one is saturated?
[10:59] Samir: Yes — smart routing can route by latency/cost/region. For Private customers with VPC constraints, cross-region routing requires networking config; we'll include a pattern doc.
[11:09] Ibrahim: We have strict data residency for EU shipments; can't route EU data outside region. So local prewarm sizing is mandatory for EU.
[11:16] Samir: Understood. We'll separate regional sims.
[11:20] Priya: What about real-time metrics? We need token-level breakdown and per-route p95.
[11:26] Lina: Redwood Console surfaces token burn, per-model latency breakdown, and route drilling. We can instrument custom tracing hooks.
[11:33] Devon: For the pilot, we're ok with 2 reserved GPUs in US and 1 in EU for a start. But we need the sim to justify that.
[11:40] Samir: We'll simulate that exact config. Two more items: (1) prewarm retention — how long do GPUs stay prewarmed during idle times? You can set idle-time thresholds; longer retention increases cost but reduces warmups. (2) backpressure signaling — Redwood can return Retry-After headers or structured hints so client SDKs backoff gracefully.
[11:58] Marta: We prefer Retry-After and a short model fallback chain.
[12:02] Samir: Noted. Any other technical nitty-gritty?
[12:08] Ibrahim: Network egress — if snapshots are in S3 inside VPC, fine. But snapshot restore parallelism could saturate network. Do you cap restore bandwidth?
[12:16] Lina: Yes, we cap restore concurrency and bandwidth; workbook includes restore-time as parameter. We can also prefetch critical keys only.
[12:25] Marta: Could you also show a scenario where KV hit ratio is low — what's the cost to reach target?
[12:30] Samir: We'll include low, medium, high KV hit scenarios. Big difference: with high KV hits, p95 drops by >40% vs cold cache.
[12:38] [12:50] (brief pause)
[13:00] Samir: Ok I'll summarize recommended pilot config from today's discussion: US: 2 reserved GPUs, prewarm 1-2 replicas, concurrency cap 4, queue window 200ms, fallback to quantized small model. EU: 1 reserved GPU, same caps but regional-only routing. We'll run sims across +/- 2x burst and 9x stress-case.
[13:23] Marta: That sounds reasonable. Please make the workbook show $ delta vs our current spend line.
[13:28] Samir: Will do.
[13:31] Priya: One operational question — who owns rollback if regression appears in quantized path?
[13:36] Lina: We'll provide an automated rollback trigger; ownership depends on your support tier — standard vs enterprise. For pilot Redwood can act on triggers with explicit permission.
[13:46] Devon: Any guidance on telemetry retention for debugging warmups? We might want 30 days of traces for incidents.
[13:52] Samir: Console supports configurable retention; for incident analysis we recommend 30-90 days. There's an add-on for long-term retention.
[14:00] Marta: OK, let's capture next steps.
[14:03] Avery: Recap: Redwood sends burst sim workbook + instructions (Samir). Cerulean sends 14-day traces and payloads (Marta). We schedule follow-up to review sims on 2026-03-12 provisional. Any objections?
[14:15] Marta: None. Thanks.
[14:17] Ibrahim: Quick: can we get the architecture doc for Private KMS/HSM?
[14:20] Samir: Yes, I'll drop the doc in the shared workspace and link in CRM.
[14:25] Avery: Thanks all. We'll follow up via email with artifacts.
